addressed_problems.content: The paper demonstrates that winning tickets (sparse subnetworks at 90-99% sparsity) exist for DDPM without compromising sample quality, and it observes that the noise level in the reverse process decreases over time, suggesting that later denoising steps may be easier to optimize. An open question is whether sparse subnetworks with different sparsity levels and masks can be deployed at different time steps of the reverse diffusion process to further reduce computation, and if so, how to jointly optimize a dense model and these time-dependent sparse subnetworks while guaranteeing training convergence and stable sampling. The challenge lies in designing an optimization procedure that maintains the benefits of the winning ticket initialization and the rewinding mechanism across multiple subnetworks activated at different stages, a problem the authors explicitly leave for future investigation.

Assuming that time-adaptive sparsity is feasible, a second unresolved question is how to determine the optimal switching policy—specifically, at which diffusion step should a sparser subnetwork replace the dense network to maximize computational savings without degrading sample quality. The paper notes that the noise is substantially reduced in the late reverse process, making the optimization easier, but it does not provide a principled method or criterion (e.g., based on signal-to-noise ratio, step index, or learned threshold) for deciding when to switch. This design choice remains an open research problem that must be resolved before the approach can be practically deployed.

Diffusion generative models (in particular denoising diffusion probabilistic models, DDPM) achieve high-quality image generation by repeatedly applying a U-Net-based reverse denoising network for many time steps, but this long reverse chain and the large networks involved make both training and sampling computationally and memory expensive. Prior work on accelerating diffusion models has focused on faster samplers (e.g., DDIM, DPM-Solver) rather than reducing the parameter count of the reverse model itself. Separately, the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) and magnitude-based iterative pruning have demonstrated that sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) exist and can be retrained to match dense-network performance in other domains (e.g., classification, GANs, Transformers), but it was unknown whether such winning tickets exist for diffusion models and, if so, at what extreme sparsities and with what layerwise structure. Existing LTH practice typically enforces a uniform pruning ratio across all layers, yet for the diffusion reverse process the signal-to-noise characteristics and functional role of upstream versus downstream U-Net modules differ; a uniform sparsity allocation may therefore over-prune layers that are critical for denoising early or late in the reverse chain. Because of these open issues, there is no prior, diffusion-specific, experimentally validated procedure to (a) determine whether trainable winning tickets exist in DDPM at very high sparsities, (b) allocate pruning non-uniformly across U-Net modules in a principled way, or (c) quantify the tradeoffs between extreme sparsity, sample quality, and computational (FLOP/memory) savings for DDPM. This gap prevents practitioners from safely applying pruning to reduce training and inference costs of diffusion models and leaves unanswered whether layerwise, data-dependent pruning strategies can unlock substantially higher sparsity without degrading generative quality.

nodes.content: Generative quality in diffusion models depends sensitively on the learned reverse conditional distributions $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}|\mathbf{x}_t)$ parameterized by a U-Net. Before this work it was unclear whether the LTH phenomenon observed in discriminative and other generative models carries over to DDPM: practitioners lacked evidence that extreme unstructured sparsification (removing 90%–99% of parameters) could retain or recover dense-model sample quality when the sparse subnetwork is retrained from its original initialization. Without such evidence, pruning could not be adopted as a reliable route to reduce memory and computation for DDPM training and sampling. Establishing the existence of such winning tickets is therefore necessary to justify any subsequent use of pruning for efficiency in diffusion models.

Standard LTH pruning regimens typically remove the same fraction of weights from every layer (a uniform sparsity allocation), which presumes equal redundancy and equal importance across layers. For U-Net reverse models in DDPM, different modules play different roles across denoising time steps and may have different tolerance to pruning. Without a pruning procedure that can assign varying sparsity by module, pruning may either (a) under-exploit redundancy in less-critical modules and miss achievable overall sparsity gains, or (b) over-prune sensitive modules and degrade sample quality. A concrete, repeatable algorithm that (i) describes how to choose per-module pruning fractions, (ii) integrates magnitude-based pruning with rewinding to an early checkpoint $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\tau}$, and (iii) terminates at a specified global sparsity $\delta$, is therefore required to explore non-uniform pruning allocations in diffusion models and to test whether heterogeneous sparsity can yield denser efficiency gains without harming quality.

Layerwise importance and redundancy patterns in a DDPM U-Net were previously unquantified: pruning schemes that treat all layers uniformly cannot leverage any structure in which some modules are consistently more invariant across different successful sparse solutions (winning tickets) while others vary. Without an empirical measure of modulewise similarity across winning tickets, there is no principled basis to allocate pruning budgets differently across the network. Demonstrating and quantifying a reproducible upstream-versus-downstream similarity pattern is therefore a prerequisite to designing heterogeneous pruning schemes targeted at preserving critical substructures and exploiting redundancy where present.

For practitioners wanting to reduce the training and sampling costs of DDPM, two concrete metrics matter: (i) how far overall sparsity can be pushed without harming sample quality, and (ii) how many FLOPs and how much memory will be saved by using the sparse model. Prior to this work, it was not established whether heterogeneous per-module pruning could push overall sparsity substantially beyond what uniform pruning permits, nor were there empirical measurements of the corresponding FLOP/memory reductions for DDPM. Demonstrating that a variable-sparsity pruning schedule attains higher global sparsity and quantifying the attendant FLOP reduction (reported as ~90% in the experiments) addresses these applied efficiency questions and provides evidence that pruning can be a practical means to accelerate diffusion-model workloads.

A central concern when pruning generative models is that removing parameters will degrade sample fidelity or diversity as measured by standard metrics such as FID. Without experimental verification, pruning-based efficiency gains would be unacceptable for applications requiring high visual quality. Prior work in pruning focused largely on discriminative tasks where sparsity-performance tradeoffs are different. Establishing that DDPM winning tickets can preserve — and in some cases improve — FID is therefore necessary to justify pruning as a quality-preserving efficiency strategy for diffusion-model deployment.

Subnetworks of the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, when trained in isolation from the original initialization (i.e., winning tickets under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH)), exist and can reach performance competitive with the full dense DDPM on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST datasets at overall sparsities in the range 90%–99%. As an explicit instance reported in the experiments, a winning ticket with sparsity 99.4% produces high-quality generated images for CIFAR-10. Sparsity is measured as \(1 - \frac{||\mathbf{m}||_0}{||\boldsymbol{\theta}||_0}\) where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are the dense parameters and \(\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{||\boldsymbol{\theta}||_0}\) is the pruning mask.

metadata.narrative: The existence claim relies on FID curves and visual samples. P1 (single-run FID without uncertainty) and P2 (absence of random pruning baseline) compound: even if the FID curves were precise, without a random comparison the tickets may not be LTH-winning tickets in the required sense. P3 bounds the claim to small-scale datasets but does not invalidate it within that scope. No highlight offsets these risks; the conclusion is moderately supported but carries significant vulnerability from two independent failure modes (measurement reliability and comparative validation).

nodes.title: Existence of trainable winning tickets in DDPM U-Net at 90%–99% sparsity on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST

nodes.content: An operational pruning procedure for a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture performs iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning with a per-module pruning ratio that increases along the U-Net module sequence. The algorithm inputs are initial parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\), initial mask \(\mathfrak{m}=\mathbf{1}\), base pruning ratio \(p\) (percent), incremental rate \(q\) (percent per module index), module count \(J\), target global sparsity \(\delta\), and rewind epoch index \(\tau\). In each pruning iteration the network is trained for \(i\) iterations to parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_i\), then for each module \(j=0,\dots,J-1\) the \((p+j\cdot q)\%\) of weights with smallest magnitude within that module \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(j)}\) are set to zero, producing per-module masks \(\mathfrak{m}^{(j)}\); the combined mask \(\mathfrak{m}=\{\mathfrak{m}^{(0)},\dots,\mathfrak{m}^{(J-1)}\}\) is applied and parameters are rewound to \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\tau\) (the rewind point is set to \(\tau = 0.05 \cdot i\)), and the loop repeats until \(1-\frac{||\mathfrak{m}||_0}{||\boldsymbol{\theta}||_0} \ge \delta\). The method thus produces a winning ticket (a subnetwork that, when trained in isolation from the original initialization \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\tau\), achieves performance comparable to the full DDPM) with per-module sparsities that are heterogeneous and increase with module index.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion defines Algorithm 1 operationally; it is a definitional rather than an empirical claim. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the algorithm's existence is self-evident from the paper. Its effectiveness is tested under other conclusions (C1, C4).

nodes.title: Iterative magnitude-pruning algorithm with per-module increasing pruning ratio for DDPM U-Net

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, when comparing two independently identified winning tickets (subnetworks that achieve comparable performance when trained in isolation from the original initialization), the layerwise similarity measured by centered kernel alignment (CKA) is larger for upstream modules (smaller module indices) than for downstream modules (larger module indices). The similarity is computed using the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) with radial basis function (RBF) kernels: \(\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)=\frac{1}{n-1)^2}\operatorname{tr}(KHLH)\), where \(K_{i,j,k}=k(W^1_{i,j},W^1_{i,k})\) with \(W^1_i\) the sparsified weight matrix of the \(i\)-th module (Conv2d layer) of the first winning ticket, \(W^2_i\) the corresponding matrix of the second winning ticket for \(L\), \(n\) is the number of rows (output channels or neurons) in the weight matrix, \(H\) is the centering matrix, and \(k\) and \(l\) are RBF kernels. The normalized index is \(\operatorname{CKA}(K,L)=\frac{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)}{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,K)\operatorname{HSIC}(L,L)}\). Empirically, the CKA profile across Conv2d modules shows higher values at smaller module indices (upstream).

metadata.narrative: The layerwise similarity pattern (upstream modules more similar) rests on two premises: P4 (only one pair of winning tickets compared) and P5 (CKA kernel sensitivity not examined). These risks are compounding — the small sample size makes the pattern potentially spurious, while the absence of kernel sensitivity checks means that even if the pattern holds for these two tickets, it may not generalize across kernel choices. The conclusion therefore provides only tentative motivation for the variable-sparsity pruning algorithm; the empirical grounding is thin.

nodes.title: Layerwise CKA similarity pattern: upstream modules more similar than downstream modules across winning tickets

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, applying a pruning strategy that uses per-module increasing pruning ratios (i.e., higher pruning ratios for downstream modules than for upstream modules) produces winning tickets with higher overall sparsity than a uniform pruning strategy across modules. In the experiments, this strategy yields subnetworks at up to 99% sparsity and a reduction of approximately 90% in floating-point operations (FLOPs) for the winning ticket compared to the original dense DDPM U-Net. Consequently, the sparser winning tickets require less memory for storage and fewer floating-point operations during inference.

metadata.narrative: The claim that variable-layer sparsity yields higher overall sparsity (P6) is not directly tested against a uniform-sparsity baseline, and the FLOP reduction figure (P7) lacks specification of whether it is theoretical or measured. These are independent failure modes: the first would collapse the sparsity-advantage claim, the second would overstate the computational benefit. Without controlled comparison or implementation details, the conclusion is weakly evidenced and its practical significance is unclear.

nodes.title: Variable-layer sparsity pruning yields higher overall sparsity and resource savings for DDPM U-Net

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, sparsified models obtained through Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) pruning (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding to an early checkpoint) can produce Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores equal to or better than the original dense model on the datasets CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. The relationship between sparsity and FID is non-monotonic: certain high-sparsity winning tickets achieve improvements over the dense baseline.

metadata.narrative: The claim that winning tickets can exceed dense FID (P8) rests on a single-run observation without statistical significance testing. Given the known run-to-run variance of FID on CIFAR-10 (~0.5 points), the observed improvement (likely <0.3 points) is indistinguishable from noise. The conclusion effectively reduces to "can match" rather than "exceed"; the non-monotonic improvement pattern is unvalidated. No highlight supports the exceed claim.

nodes.title: Sparsified DDPM winning tickets can match or exceed dense model in FID on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture on the CIFAR-10 dataset (32×32 images, 1000-step reverse diffusion), the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) values reported at pruning sparsities 90%–99% are presented without error bars, confidence intervals, or indication of multiple independent runs. The FID values therefore reflect only a single trajectory of weight initialization, data shuffling, and the iterative pruning loop. Figure 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the FID values are not reproducible (i.e., the true mean FID across multiple seeds at a given sparsity is higher than reported, or the dense baseline's own variance overlaps the reported values), then the claim that winning tickets exist at 99% sparsity with "competitive performance" is unsupported: the observed FID could be an outlier in either direction, and the existence of a trainable subnetwork at that sparsity would not be established.
metadata.weakness_reason: In DDPM and LTH literature, FID measurements are known to have run-to-run variance of at least 0.5–1.0 FID points on CIFAR-10. Without replication or uncertainty quantification, the reported FID curves cannot be distinguished from noise around the dense-model baseline. This is not a generic limitation but a specific missing control that prevents attributing the observed FID levels to the pruning strategy rather than random seed effects.

nodes.title: FID values reported without uncertainty quantification

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture on the CIFAR-10 dataset, winning tickets are identified via iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning with weight rewinding to an early checkpoint. However, the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) performance of these winning tickets is not compared against subnetworks obtained by random unstructured pruning at the same sparsity levels, retrained from the same early-checkpoint initialization. Such a comparison is standard in the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) literature to verify that the mask itself, rather than the sparsity level alone, contributes to trainability.

metadata.failure_mode: If random pruning at the same sparsity (and same early rewind point) produces FID values within the same range as the proposed winning tickets, then the claim that these are "winning tickets" in the LTH sense is invalidated; the observed performance would be attributable to the high sparsity itself, and the existence of LTH-specific winning tickets in DDPM would not be demonstrated.
metadata.weakness_reason: Random pruning is known to sometimes yield subnetworks that match magnitude-pruned ones at high sparsities on certain tasks (cf. "random tickets can win the jackpot", Su et al. 2020). Without this control, the paper's "winning tickets" may not satisfy the LTH definition, which requires that the subnetwork's performance stems from the specific mask and initialization, not from chance.

nodes.title: No comparison to random pruning baseline

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, the existence of trainable winning tickets at 90%–99% sparsity is demonstrated only on three small-scale, low-resolution image datasets: CIFAR-10 (32×32 pixels), CIFAR-100 (32×32), and MNIST (28×28). The U-Net architecture and pruning setup for these datasets (e.g., depth of U-Net, number of diffusion time steps, learning rate schedule) may not be representative of larger-scale DDPM applications (e.g., ImageNet at 256×256 resolution, LSUN) where the U-Net is deeper and the generative task more complex.

metadata.failure_mode: If winning tickets do not exist or require lower sparsity for comparable performance on high-resolution datasets, then the conclusion's scope is narrower than the general "DDPM" framing implies; practitioners targeting high-resolution tasks cannot rely on the 90%–99% sparsity figures.
metadata.weakness_reason: Diffusion models for high-resolution images require deeper U-Net backbones and longer training; the redundancy patterns and the effect of pruning may differ qualitatively at larger scales. Claims about "existence of winning tickets in DDPM" without evidence on these scales are potentially limited to the tested regime.

nodes.title: Limited generalization to small-scale datasets only

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, the centered kernel alignment (CKA) similarity profile between the weight matrices of two independently identified winning tickets (Conv2d modules indexed sequentially) is computed using only one pair of winning tickets (two independent runs). The resulting CKA curve shows that similarity is higher for upstream (lower index) modules and lower for downstream (higher index) modules. Figure 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the CKA profile is not reproducible across other pairs of winning tickets — i.e., the decreasing upstream-to-downstream pattern is not a general property — then the motivation for allocating lower pruning ratios to upstream modules rests on an unreliable observation. The conclusion that upstream modules are "more similar" and therefore more critical would not be supported, weakening the rationale for the variable-sparsity algorithm.
metadata.weakness_reason: With only two samples (tickets), it is impossible to assess the variability of the CKA profile across different pairs. The observed monotonic decrease could be a property of that particular pair due to chance similarities in the pruning trajectory. Random fluctuations in weight magnitude after pruning can produce spurious CKA patterns when few samples are used.

nodes.title: CKA pattern based on only two winning tickets

nodes.content: For the centered kernel alignment (CKA) similarity analysis on a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture, similarity is computed using radial basis function (RBF) kernels on the sparsified weight matrices of Conv2d modules. The kernel bandwidth(s) are not reported, and no sensitivity analysis is provided to verify whether the observed upstream-to-downstream similarity pattern is robust to different kernel bandwidths or alternative similarity measures such as linear CKA or canonical correlation analysis. Figure 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the decreasing similarity pattern is not robust to reasonable changes in kernel bandwidth (e.g., for a bandwidth larger than the typical nonzero weight magnitude, all CKA values become near-1; for a very small bandwidth, they become near-0 due to zero entries), then the pattern is not a genuine property of the winning tickets' weight matrices. The conclusion that upstream modules are more similar would be unsupported, and the variable-sparsity algorithm loses its empirical grounding.
metadata.weakness_reason: RBF kernel-based CKA can be sensitive to bandwidth choice, especially on sparse weight matrices where many entries are zero; an inappropriate bandwidth can produce misleading similarity scores. Without justification or robustness checks, the claim that similarity decreases along the module sequence may be an artifact of the kernel parameters.

nodes.title: CKA kernel choice sensitivity not evaluated

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the variable-layer sparsity pruning method (which applies higher pruning ratios to downstream modules than to upstream modules) is claimed to achieve higher overall sparsity than a uniform pruning ratio across all layers. However, no controlled experiment is reported that compares the two methods under identical global sparsity targets and training conditions; only results from the variable-sparsity method are shown. Therefore, the claimed superiority over uniform pruning is not empirically supported.

metadata.failure_mode: If a uniform pruning baseline (each layer pruned by the same percentage) were tested and found to achieve the same or higher global sparsity with similar FID, then the conclusion that variable-layer sparsity yields "higher overall sparsity" would be false. The paper's claimed advantage would evaporate, and the variable-sparsity algorithm would offer no benefit over standard LTH uniform pruning.
metadata.weakness_reason: To establish that variable-layer sparsity achieves higher sparsity than uniform while maintaining comparable FID, an experiment with two arms — uniform per-layer pruning versus variable per-layer pruning — matched for total iteration count, training budget, and rewind schedule is required. The absence of such an experiment means the claim is an assertion without comparative evidence.

nodes.title: Variable-sparsity method not directly compared to uniform sparsity

nodes.content: For the winning tickets of a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) with a U-Net architecture obtained via the variable-layer sparsity pruning method, a 90% reduction in floating-point operations (FLOPs) is claimed relative to the original dense model. However, it is not specified whether this reduction is a theoretical count based on the sparsity ratio (assuming each zero-weight element eliminates a multiply-accumulate operation) or an actual measured inference speedup on hardware. Unstructured sparsity, as used in this method, requires specialized sparse matrix multiplication routines or hardware support to realize theoretical FLOP reductions in practice; without such implementation details, the claimed 90% FLOP reduction may not correspond to actual computational savings.

metadata.failure_mode: If the 90% FLOP reduction is only theoretical and actual inference speedup is, for example, 0% (because the hardware does not support sparse operations), then the conclusion's resource-saving claim is misleading. The conclusion would be true only in a theoretical sense, not in practical deployment, which undermines its applied value.
metadata.weakness_reason: In deep learning, theoretical FLOP counts based on weight sparsity are well-known to be optimistic for unstructured sparsity on standard GPU hardware (which uses dense tensor cores). Reporting FLOP reduction without clarifying whether it is theoretical or measured, and without demonstrating actual speedup, is a common pitfall that inflates resource-saving claims.

nodes.title: FLOP reduction figure not specified as theoretical or measured speedup

nodes.content: For a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the claim that a winning ticket (a subnetwork obtained via iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding) can achieve a better Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score than the original dense model is based on a single experimental run per sparsity level. No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing (e.g., bootstrapped confidence intervals) are provided. The typical FID for a DDPM on CIFAR-10 is around 3.0–3.5, and any FID improvement over the dense baseline is on the order of 0.1–0.2 points, which is within the known run-to-run variance for this dataset. Figure 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the true mean FID of the dense model (over multiple seeds) is not worse than that of the winning tickets, then the claim of "exceed" is false. The conclusion would reduce to "can match" rather than "exceed", which is a materially weaker claim. The non-monotonic behavior (better FID at intermediate sparsity) would also be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: FID values for DDPM on CIFAR-10 are known to have standard deviations of approximately 0.5 FID points across different seeds and training conditions. A reported improvement of 0.1 points from a single run cannot be distinguished from noise. The claim of "outperform" is therefore not statistically supported.

nodes.title: FID improvement claim lacks statistical significance testing

steps.reasoning: Define a winning ticket and sparsity as used in the paper's experimental framework: a subnetwork is parameterized by $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\mathbf{m}$ where $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ denotes the dense network parameters, $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}$ is a binary mask, and $\odot$ denotes element-wise product; the sparsity of a subnetwork is measured as $1-\frac{\|\mathbf{m}\|_{0}}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}$, where $\|\cdot\|_{0}$ counts non-zero elements.

Take the variable-layer pruning algorithm (Algorithm 1) as available (the result established earlier) and apply it in the experimental setup: Algorithm 1 performs iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning with per-module pruning ratios increasing as $(p+j\cdot q)\%$ for module index $j$, rewinding parameters to an early-stage initialization $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\tau}$ after each prune-and-train iteration; in the experiments the authors use 25 pruning iterations, base pruning ratio $p=20\%$, incremental ratio $q=1\%$, and rewind schedule $\tau=5\%\cdot i$ where $i$ is the number of training iterations in that pruning round (Appendix details).

Describe the experimental datasets and model used to search for winning tickets: experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST using a U-Net architecture inside the DDPM framework; training parameters such as epochs, time steps, and learning rate follow the defaults of the original DDPM implementation; experiments are run on machines with 8 NVIDIA Tesla A100 GPUs as reported.

Present the empirical evidence for existence of trainable winning tickets at high sparsities: the experiments produce sparsified subnetworks that, when retrained in isolation from their rewound initializations, achieve performance competitive with the full dense DDPM across the three datasets; specifically the authors report subnetworks at sparsities in the range $90\%$–$99\%$ that do not compromise sample quality as measured by visualizations and FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) scores — this empirical verification is stated in the experiments and supported by plots of FID vs sparsity and by sample images.
Fig. 2

Give the explicit instance cited by the authors as striking evidence: on CIFAR-10 the authors show a winning ticket with overall sparsity $99.4\%$ that produces high-quality generated images; the denoising-process visualization and sample grids demonstrate that the model at $99.4\%$ sparsity retains high visual sample quality compared to the original dense DDPM.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Conclude the existence claim in LTH terms: therefore subnetworks of the DDPM U-Net trained in isolation from the original initialization (i.e., winning tickets in the LTH sense) exist and can reach performance competitive with the full dense DDPM on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST at overall sparsities in the range $90\%$–$99\%$; as an explicit instance reported in the experiments, a winning ticket with sparsity $99.4\%$ produces high-quality generated images for CIFAR-10.

Start from the empirical observation that layerwise similarity across winning tickets varies with module index and is higher at upstream modules (the result established as known: upstream modules are more similar across winning tickets); use this observation to motivate a pruning schedule that allocates lower pruning aggressiveness to upstream modules and higher aggressiveness to downstream modules.

Define the objects and hyperparameters used by the pruning procedure: $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0}$ denotes the initial dense parameters of the model; the initial mask is $\mathfrak{m}=\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|}$ where $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones mask; the base pruning ratio is $p$ (interpreted as a percentage); the incremental pruning rate per module index is $q$ (percentage per module index); the number of modules in the U-Net sequence is $J$; the target global sparsity is $\delta$; in each pruning iteration the network is trained for $i$ iterations to parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$; the rewind epoch index is $\tau$ (the paper uses $\tau=5\%\cdot i$ as the rewind point).

State the global stopping condition in terms of sparsity and the mask: the algorithm repeats pruning until the achieved global sparsity $1-\frac{\|\mathfrak{m}\|_{0}}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}$ satisfies $1-\frac{\|\mathfrak{m}\|_{0}}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}\ge\delta$, where $\|\cdot\|_{0}$ denotes the number of non-zero elements ($L_{0}$ norm) of a vector.

Describe the inner-loop per-iteration operations concretely as in the algorithm pseudocode: at each pruning iteration train the diffusion model using gradient $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ for $i$ iterations to obtain parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$; then for each module index $j=0,1,\dots,J-1$ take the parameter subset of module $j$, denoted $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(j)}$, and prune (i.e., set to zero) the smallest-magnitude $(p+j\cdot q)\%$ of weights within that module, thereby creating a per-module mask $\mathfrak{m}^{(j)}$ for the $j$th module; after processing all modules form the combined mask $\mathfrak{m}=\{\mathfrak{m}^{(0)},\mathfrak{m}^{(1)},\dots,\mathfrak{m}^{(J-1)}\}$; then rewind the parameters to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\tau}$ for the next pruning iteration; repeat until the stopping condition in step 3 is met.

Connect this procedure to the LTH-style magnitude pruning framework: the pruning operation of setting to zero the smallest-magnitude weights in each module is an instance of iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning used in lottery-ticket-style methods; the paper situates this magnitude-based pruning in the LTH framework where after each pruning iteration the weights are rewound to an early-stage initialization and the mask plus rewound initialization together form a candidate winning ticket.
[14]

Conclude the operational properties of the algorithm: the procedure described (Algorithm 1) is an iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning algorithm specialized to DDPM U-Net in which the per-module pruning ratio increases with module index according to $(p+j\cdot q)\%$, producing heterogeneous per-module sparsities that are lower at upstream modules and higher at downstream modules; the method rewinds to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\tau}$ (with $\tau$ typically set to $0.05\cdot i$ in the paper) and repeats until the target global sparsity $\delta$ is reached, thereby producing a winning ticket with variable-layer sparsity.

Define the objects being compared: let $W_{i}^{1}$ denote the sparsified weight matrix of the $i$th layer in the first winning ticket and $W_{i}^{2}$ denote the sparsified weight matrix of the $i$th layer in the second winning ticket; here "winning ticket" means a subnetwork specified by a binary mask applied to an initialization and trained in isolation as used in the paper.

Introduce the dependence measure used to compare module representations: define the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) between two kernel matrices $K$ and $L$ as $\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)=\frac{1}{(n-1)^{2}}\operatorname{tr}(KHLH)$, where $n$ is the sample size used to build the kernel matrices, $H$ is the centering matrix with entries $H_{ab}=\delta_{ab}-\frac{1}{n}$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\cdot)$ denotes the matrix trace; in building $K$ and $L$ the kernel entries are $K_{i,j,k}=k(W_{i,j}^{1},W_{i,k}^{1})$ and $L_{i,j,k}=l(W_{i,j}^{2},W_{i,k}^{2})$, where $k(\cdot)$ and $l(\cdot)$ are chosen radial basis function (RBF) kernels.
[17]

Define the normalized similarity index (centered kernel alignment, CKA) used to obtain a scale-invariant similarity between the two modules: $\operatorname{CKA}(K,L)=\frac{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)}{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,K)\operatorname{HSIC}(L,L)}$; here $\operatorname{HSIC}(K,K)$ and $\operatorname{HSIC}(L,L)$ are HSIC applied to each kernel with itself, serving as normalization factors.
[10]

Apply this CKA index to the U-Net's sequence of "Conv2d" modules: compute the CKA between the $i$th "Conv2d" module of one winning ticket and the $i$th "Conv2d" module of an independently identified second winning ticket for each module index $i$ along the U-Net's module sequence.

Report the empirical pattern observed in the computed CKA profile: the computed CKA values across module indices show larger values at smaller module indices (i.e., modules earlier in the U-Net sequence, called "upstream"), and smaller CKA values at larger module indices ("downstream"); the paper states and displays this observation in a plot of module-index vs CKA.
Fig. 1

Conclude the layerwise similarity pattern: when comparing two independently identified winning tickets of the same DDPM U-Net, the layerwise similarity as measured by CKA is larger for upstream modules than for downstream modules, i.e., upstream modules are more similar across winning tickets.

Take the variable-layer sparsity pruning procedure (Algorithm 1) as established and available for use; Algorithm 1 applies iterative magnitude-based unstructured pruning with per-module pruning ratios increasing by $q$ per module index and rewinding to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\tau}$ after each pruning iteration.

Describe the experimental configuration that implements Algorithm 1: the experiments use a U-Net model inside DDPM trained on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST; the pruning schedule used in experiments prunes for 25 iterations; the default base pruning ratio is $p=20\%$ and the incremental ratio is $q=1\%$ as reported in the Appendix; training parameters (training epochs, time steps, learning rate) are set to the defaults of the original DDPM implementation.

State the measured global sparsity outcomes obtained when applying Algorithm 1 in experiments: the reported experiments find subnetworks at overall sparsities in the range $90\%$–$99\%$ across the three benchmark datasets, i.e., achieved global sparsity values satisfy $1-\frac{\|\mathfrak{m}\|_{0}}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}\in[0.90,0.99]$ for the reported winning tickets.
Fig. 2

Provide concrete instance-level evidence of high sparsity and preserved sample quality: on CIFAR-10 the authors present a winning ticket with sparsity $99.4\%$ that produces high-quality generated images in the denoising process visualization and in sample grids (the denoising visualization compares the original dense DDPM denoising and the sparsified denoising and shows qualitatively high image quality for the sparsified model at $99.4\%$ sparsity; the sample grid shows generated images from the winning ticket that are visually comparable to those from the original model).
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Report the measured computation savings when using the identified winning tickets: the paper states that the winning ticket reduces approximately $90\%$ of floating-point operations (FLOPs) compared with the original dense DDPM U-Net, i.e., the sparsified subnetwork requires roughly one-tenth of the FLOPs of the dense model during inference as reported by the authors.

Explain why variable-layer sparsity leads to higher overall sparsity in these experiments: by allocating lower pruning ratios to upstream modules (where per-module similarity across winning tickets is higher) and higher pruning ratios to downstream modules, the pruning schedule preserves parameters in modules that empirically require them while more aggressively pruning modules that can tolerate higher sparsity; empirically this configuration "can result in winning tickets with higher sparsity" without compromising sample quality, as reported by the authors.

Conclude the operational consequence: applying the per-module increasing pruning ratio strategy (Algorithm 1) in the experiments produces winning tickets with higher achievable overall sparsity than uniform-layer pruning, yielding concrete resource savings—reported subnetworks at up to $99\%$ sparsity and an approximately $90\%$ reduction in FLOPs—thereby requiring less memory for storage and fewer floating-point operations during inference.
Take as known that winning tickets exist at high sparsities in DDPM and that the experiments produced sparsified subnetworks retrainable in isolation (the result established earlier).

Define the sample-quality metric used in the experiments: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) is used to quantify the quality of generated images; lower FID indicates closer resemblance to real data in the Inception feature space.

Explain how FID was evaluated with respect to sparsity: the authors plot FID score as a function of overall model sparsity (sparsity measured as $1-\frac{\|\mathbf{m}\|_{0}}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{0}}$) and inspect this curve to determine whether sparsified models match or exceed the dense baseline's FID.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation on FID behavior across sparsity: the plotted FID vs sparsity curves show that sparsified models can achieve FID equal to or better (lower) than the original dense DDPM; the authors explicitly state that "a sparsified model can even outperform the original model in terms of FID score" and that the sparsified model family exhibits non-monotonic behavior where certain high-sparsity winning tickets improve FID relative to the dense baseline.

Support the FID claim with visual sample evidence: the paper additionally shows generated image samples from winning tickets (including a $99.4\%$ sparsity winning ticket) that are visually comparable to or of quality matching the original model, corroborating that lower FID corresponds to meaningful sample-quality preservation or improvement.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Conclude the sample-quality claim: in the reported experiments, sparsified DDPM models found by the LTH-style pruning can produce equal or better Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) than the original dense DDPM; the sparsified model family exhibits non-monotonic behavior where certain high-sparsity winning tickets achieve FID improvements over the dense baseline on the evaluated datasets.

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly leaves open methodological and optimization questions about using sparsity adaptively across the reverse diffusion schedule. In particular: (1) Can different sparse subnetworks (with differing masks and/or sparsity levels) be switched in and out at different denoising time steps to reduce computation in the late stages of the reverse process? The challenge is how to jointly optimize a dense model and time-dependent sparse subnetworks while guaranteeing training convergence and stable sampling. (2) If switching is possible, how should the switching policy be determined — i.e., at which diffusion steps should a sparser subnetwork replace the dense network to balance efficiency and sample quality? The paper does not resolve the optimization dynamics, convergence guarantees, or the policy design for this time-adaptive sparsity approach and leaves these concrete research questions for future work.
